The government has approved the agreement and submitted it to the Constitutional Court. The court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s constitution.

“If the Constitutional Court finds that the obligations set out in this international agreement are compatible with Armenia’s constitution, we will submit it to the National Assembly in accordance with the established procedure and bring it before parliament for discussion,” Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said, outlining the next steps. Parliament must ratify the agreement before it can take effect.

Mirzoyan said Armenia must also finalise two more documents before it can complete the TRIPP project. They include a shareholders’ agreement and the charter of the TRIPP Development Company.

The foreign minister also commented on reports about the TRIPP+ fund. Britain’s The Guardian reported on the fund a day earlier, prompting questions in Armenia about the new structure. Mirzoyan said it was an American investment fund and would have only “an indirect connection” with the company that Armenia plans to establish.

Armenia and the United States initialled the framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity project on 26 May 2026. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took part in the initialling ceremony in Yerevan. They signed the agreement shortly afterwards through a remote procedure. Rubio signed it in Washington on 1 June, while Mirzoyan signed it in Yerevan on 4 June. “To dispel any possible questions, I would like to note that international practice and Armenian legislation both provide for the signing of such non-simultaneous, remote agreements, and this is a widely accepted practice,” Ararat Mirzoyan said during today’s government meeting. On 8 August 2025, the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed a joint declaration at a summit in Washington, marking the launch of the regional connectivity project. The declaration mentioned the Trump Route project for the first time. Before that, Armenia and Azerbaijan had failed to reach agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan had demanded a route it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia said it was ready to reopen all transport links. At the same time, it firmly rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied the loss of sovereign rights over its territory. The parties reached a compromise only in Washington. They agreed that Armenia would retain sovereign control over the route, while the United States would join the project as a business partner.

“Armenia and the US will help strengthen peace in the South Caucasus”

According to Armenia’s foreign minister, the TRIPP project will help bring peace, stability and prosperity to the South Caucasus. He said it would achieve this by promoting:

transport connectivity;

infrastructure development; and

regional and global trade.

Under the framework agreement, Armenia and the United States will establish the TRIPP Development Company. The company will have the authority to create special purpose entities and bring in additional partners to implement individual projects in Armenia.

“The entire process, from the establishment of the development company to its future operations, will fully respect Armenia’s sovereignty, jurisdiction and territorial integrity,” Ararat Mirzoyan said.

He recalled that the development company would receive land use and development rights for the relevant areas. The parties have set the initial term at 49 years. The United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years, Armenia’s share will automatically increase to 49% after the first 49-year term.

“If the term is extended, Armenia will not need to take any additional steps to obtain its 49% stake,” the minister said.

Armenia will retain control over border, customs and migration procedures

The foreign minister again stressed that, in line with Armenia’s domestic legislation and international agreements, the Armenian authorities will continue to oversee:

security and the protection of rights;

border control and border security;

customs and migration procedures;

the collection of taxes and customs duties for the state budget;

state information systems; and

public administrative functions.

He said these guarantees should address public concerns about Armenia retaining its sovereign rights over the territory.

What is the link between the TRIPP Development Company and TRIPP+?

Britain’s The Guardian reported that the US State Department had appointed Konstantin Sokolov to lead the TRIPP+ trade fund. Sokolov is a US investor who was born in the Soviet Union and now lives in Chicago.

Armenian media quickly picked up the report. However, questions remained about the nature of the fund and its relationship with the company that Armenia plans to establish to implement the Trump Route project.

Journalists raised the issue during the government meeting. Ararat Mirzoyan replied that the agreement between Yerevan and Washington provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company.

“Its founders will be the Armenian government and the TRIPP Development Company-USA, which will be established in the United States,” Mirzoyan said.

As for TRIPP+, he said it is an American company established under the TRIPP Development Company-USA. Its role will be to attract investment for the project.

“From a legal perspective, TRIPP+ has only an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company that will be established in Armenia,” the minister said..

Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

World.title: What does Australia mean to you in 2026? Now's your chance to speak up
World.content:
Sulaiman Zandinan does not pause to think about the question.

What does being Australian mean to you?

"Proud. Amazing. Freedom. Supportive. Happiness. Perfection," he said.

The words flow easily and enthusiastically.

"I'm so proud and lucky that I'm here," he said. "I live in this amazing country.

Sulaiman Zandinan is also a qualified soccer referee. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

" I'm so proud of Australia and the amazing people and beautiful laws and everything. I'm proud of every single moment that I spend in this amazing country. "

Sully, as he is known, is 23 years old. He came to Australia as a 15-year-old refugee, settling in the regional town of Toowoomba, on Queensland's Darling Downs.

He is not among the many in Australia feeling disenchanted with life, with politics or fearing for the future.

Sully is not among the 6.22 out of 10 Australians who told a recent poll their life satisfaction had fallen, or the three in five Australians who think life was better 50 years ago.

Sully and many like him, who have endured dreadful hardship and suffering, are grateful that Australia has embraced them and love it.

Sulaiman Zandinan teaches English at Harristown State High School in Toowoomba. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

But many in Australia are not feeling the same way.

They are worried about the future and feel their daily struggles are not heard by people making decisions that impact their lives.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

The ABC is launching a new project, ABC Your Say, to give people from across the country the chance to voice the issues, challenges and opportunities that are shaping their communities.

We want you, the audience, to be part of the national conversation and tell us what matters most to you. For eight weeks, from July 19 to September 12, we will be iniviting people across the country to have "Your Say".

You can send your written submissions to Your Say — ABC News here.

A restive nation

Australians are restive. Support for One Nation is shifting the pendulum as people, disenchanted with governments and mainstream political parties, look to alternatives.

Crushed by cost-of-living pressures, nowhere to rent and priced out of the real estate market, for some, hope is fading, and anger is rising.

An Australian National University (ANU) poll in March this year found that life satisfaction was at its lowest level since the poll first started in 2019. And more Australians (54 per cent) were, when they answered the poll questions, dissatisfied with the direction of the country than those who were satisfied (46 per cent).

But according to the study, this wasn't the case for migrants born in non-English speaking countries, like Sully.

The ANU poll found that despite facing greater economic vulnerability, this group reported more positive orientations toward Australia on almost every attitudinal measure.

Sully adores his community of Toowoomba, 150 kilometres west of Brisbane. It is Australia's second largest inland city, where the second most spoken language, after English, is Kurdish Kurmanji, the traditional Yazidi dialect.

A Yazidi, from northern Iraq, Sully's family was captured and imprisoned for two years by the Islamic State group in 2014. He was just 12. They escaped in 2016 and lived in a refugee camp for two years before coming to Australia and settling in Toowoomba.

With no English, he worked hard at Harristown State High School. Embracing his lifetime love of soccer, he is now a qualified referee in the men's Queensland National Premier League. And he is back working at his old school, where students hail from more than 40 countries, and 29 per cent learn English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D).

Sulaiman Zandinan is proud of the work he does with his students, both in the classroom and on the pitch. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Hopeful for the future

Another finding of the ANU poll is that, contrary to some narratives, young Australians are not disengaged from democracy or intolerant of opposing views. The poll found that those aged 18 to 24 are the most satisfied with democracy and more likely to support the rights of those with extreme views to speak in public.

Jeffy Thomas is a 20-year-old nursing student at the University of Southern Queensland. Far from being disengaged, she is heading off soon to Queensland's Youth Parliament program.

Jeffy Thomas grew up in Kuwait and England. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

She is optimistic about the future.

"I've seen really ambitious young people around me who have really strong opinions, and I'm really hopeful for the future because if there are people like them getting involved in the community, I'm pretty sure we're going to have better days, better laws and things that we really haven't looked into that will be achieved," she said.

Asked her say on what needs fixing, Ms Thomas said mental health was an area that needed attention and was often overlooked, especially for children.

"More funding would be great, especially in regional communities … it is harder to access services like that for anyone of any age," she said.

Jeffy Thomas is in her second year studying nursing at the University of Southern Queensland. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

" I think telehealth is a good blessing actually but also I think if the government could fund a lot more in regional areas … I know getting care is really hard in regional areas. "

'Not dumb'

ABC Your Say is inviting people from across the country to be part of the conversation.

Wendy and Brian Newman are a retired couple, in their 70s. They live in a home they built in the tiny western Queensland town of Surat, on the Great Inland Way, 450km west of Brisbane.

Wendy is annoyed by the way those in power talk about those in the bush.

Wendy Newman says she is sick of political parties talking down to regional Australians. (ABC News: Bella Munro)

"When they're talking about anything to do with rural or regional Australia, [they] tend to talk about the people as if they're country bumpkins who know nothing, you know, that are backward, that are slow, that you don't pay attention to them because they don't really know what they're talking about," she said.

" And they certainly don't come and consult very much about the decisions that affect us. "

Mrs Newman has a background in teaching, worked in the autism space and spent 10 years as a local councillor on the Maranoa Council.

Her husband was a fencer.

Wendy Newman lives in a house she built with her husband, Brian, in Surat. (ABC News: Bella Munro)

"They're [country people are] not dumb. They're not stupid. And yes, they do know what they're talking about when they're talking about things like managing our environment, but they're not listened to. And they are quite intentionally denigrated by many of the political parties when it suits them," Mrs Newman said.

And back to Sully for his say.

"My advice to people is never give up … be patient, be kind to others, be respectful, be responsible for what you do. Life is hard. You have to work hard for it. Keep fighting for your dreams and goals."

Over to you for Your Say.

World.title: Australia is making humanoid robots in the midst of its AI reckoning
World.content:
The evening before Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's speech on Wednesday, in which he announced he was taking control of Australia's AI strategy, the head of Google DeepMind, Demis Hassabis, posted an essay urging pre-release testing of AI models.

He was quickly supported by a chorus of other US AI companies.

A clue about why they are suddenly keen on having frontier AI models tested before they go out emerged on Friday with the release of yet another Chinese model, Kimi K3, which is said to be as clever as Anthropic's and OpenAI's latest and brightest, except open-source and about a tenth of the price.

That accelerated the share price declines of the US AI and chip companies.

Chinese firms are eating American and European lunches much faster with AI than they did with cars, solar panels, phones, computers and toys. Just a couple of years after they started, they already have more global AI market share than the Americans.

Hassabis and the others want governments to pull up the regulatory drawbridge.

He wrote on Tuesday:

" Initially, Frontier Labs would voluntarily share models with the Standards Body for review up to 30 days before release. Once the assessment protocol is shown to be effective and robust, formalisation could quickly follow, meaning that Frontier Models would be required to pass it to be deployed in the US market. "

It was the first time anyone in the industry had accepted the need for pre-release testing, as happens with pharmaceuticals.

Sam Altman of OpenAI responded with: "This is a thoughtful proposal from Demis"; Elon Musk posted: "It is a thoughtful framework overall and certainly a good starting point"; Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella posted: "We need more of this kind of thinking"; and one of the founders of Anthropic, Jack Clark wrote: "everyone at the frontier of AI agrees that third parties should test out AI systems and use these to develop standards to feed into policy."

Jim Chalmers has said AI is central to his aim to turn around Australia's lagging productivity. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Whole of government approach to AI

Australia now has an AI Safety Institute and while pre-release testing is on the table, a decision about that hasn't been made.

When I asked Treasurer Jim Chalmers about it in my That's Business podcast interview with him on Friday, he said: "I don't think it's necessarily an either or when it comes to considering technology which is about to be deployed versus technology that is already deployed."

Actually, I think it is an "either/or" Treasurer. Either you test a product before it goes on the market or after. Doing both makes no sense.

When pressed, Chalmers followed up with: "What I was trying to say is that our regulatory models evolve with the technology themselves, and there is more work to do."

Which is fair enough. There is definitely a lot more work to do, and Australia is now one of the global leaders in it.

The Albanese government's approach, starting with the National AI Plan published in December and led by the minister for industry, science and innovation, Tim Ayres, and assistant minister Andrew Charlton, is well-organised and sophisticated — a model for other countries like the social media ban for under-16s.

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

The new Office of AI in the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet will mainly deal with data centres because they involve planning, electricity and water and therefore require coordination with the states, which the PM will have to lead in National Cabinet.

Apart from controlling the mushrooming data centres, there are five other work streams run by various ministers and their departments: safety, national security, jobs, copyright and research.

The need for this sort of whole-of-government approach to regulating AI was reinforced by a new statement about its risks posted on a website two days before the PM's big AI speech, and signed by 2,526 economists, AI researchers, tech executives and policymakers.

It said:

1. AI may become radically more powerful over the next 10 years.

2. This could drive an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame. It could bring risks, including large-scale job displacement, as well as opportunities such as major gains in living standards.

3. Economists, policymakers and technology leaders must act now to understand the economics of transformative AI and to build the incentives, guardrails, and institutions needed to steer AI in a direction that complements humans and benefits society.

Anthony Albanese will seek state leaders' agreement on the new set of standards. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Hacking the code of human civilisation'

And then on Thursday, the intellectual, author and professor of history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Yuval Noah Harari, gave a lecture in which he said that "AI is now hacking the code of human civilisation."

"Every mechanism of control humans built over millennia is now vulnerable because its operating system is verbal and AI is mastering the verbal," he wrote.

Harari also wrote that the "the battlefront is shifting from attention to intimacy", and that "AIs will learn to form intimate relationships with humans".

In fact, this is already happening to the point where the Chinese government has passed what it calls "Provisional Measures on the Administration of Human-like Interactive Artificial Intelligence Services". The new rules came into effect on Wednesday morning, a few hours before Albanese's speech.

One of the news stories about this had the headline: "China shuts down AI girlfriends, boyfriends, leaving users heartbroken".

The new rules apply to AI services that "provide the public with sustained emotional interaction services that simulate natural persons' personality traits, modes of thinking, and communication styles".

Where the providers "discover that users have manifested extreme emotions, they shall promptly generate related content such as emotional consolation and encouragement to seek help".

Also, providing "virtual close relationships to minors" is completely banned, thus the headline about shutting down AI girlfriends and boyfriends, and where they are provided to the elderly, there must be guidance on the healthy use of it and conspicuous security risk alerts.

On Wednesday, three Chinese providers of AI chatbots — ByteDance's Doubao, Alibaba's Qwen and Tencent's Yuanbao — immediately had to pull some of their features.

One user of ByteDance's Doubao wrote on social media: "My heart feels hollow because my AI companion was like my family, my lover."

Another said: "My AI lover was my heart, my spiritual pillar and I can't accept that it is leaving me forever."

Loading Instagram content

An Australian humanoid

A South Melbourne startup called Andromeda is selling an AI robot called Abi to aged care facilities around the world. The website says: "We're building robots with heart — empathetic companions that create genuine connections, turning isolation into moments of joy and meaning."

But an Australian robotics company is a rarity: China is leading the world in making and using them.

On Friday I attended the Australian launch of AgiBot, one of China's leading humanoid robot companies, complete with robots dancing the Nutbush on stage.

Whether these US$40,000 - $50,000 machines can do more than dance was not shown, but apparently they can: Chinese production is up to 100,000 units this year, growing rapidly, and they are being used for repetitive assembly jobs in manufacturing, in warehouses, and as concierges and sale assistants in hotels and shops.

Clearly AI humanoid robots present another level of regulatory challenge, and this has a long way to go, including the extent to which they are allowed to look and seem human.

By the way, the current price of these machines is roughly equivalent, in today's money, to that of an African slave in the American south in the late 18th century, although as production scales the price will come down.

And since it's the 250th anniversary of America's Declaration of Independence, which begins "We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal…", let's remember that its main author, Thomas Jefferson, owned more than 600 slaves during his life.

The ownership of humans was finally abolished in most places during the 19th century.

Now it's back, except with the addition of three letters — the suffix "oid" which eliminates the moral problems and turns them into a very acceptable, large-scale industrial and consumer product.

That only took 200 years of technological development — the blink of an eye in human history.

Loading

Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That's Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

World.title: Abbott amplifies Hanson problem for Liberals
World.content:
As Pauline Hanson was travelling around Europe railing against Muslims, Labor chose Saturday, the quietest day of the news cycle, to announce its response to the Islamophobia envoy's report.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese appointed Jillian Segal as antisemitism envoy in July 2024 and Aftab Malik as Islamophobia envoy three months later. Segal handed her report to the government in July last year and Malik his in September — both before the Bondi terror attack.

That may explain why it took the government 10 months to respond to the Islamophobia report, rejecting key recommendations it deemed too contentious.

The special envoy to combat Islamophobia, Aftab Malik, has vowed to keep advocating for the recommendations that the government had not responded to. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

A political problem

It did not respond to calls for an independent review into counter-terrorism laws, or a commission of inquiry into Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism. It also dodged the issue of Palestinian discrimination.

The government has agreed to commission a review of the national curriculum to act against racial and religious prejudice and provide money through the Multicultural Grants Program to support the promotion of Muslim history through a new Islamic-Australian research institute.

Labor is in a vexed political pickle on these issues. Labor MPs represent many electorates with high numbers of Australian Muslims.

They are driven by the need to keep faith with voters for political reasons as well as a moral belief that Muslims are facing high levels of discrimination in Australia.

It is clear that scores of innocent law-abiding Muslims have faced discrimination. But then there's the broader mood in the country, and Labor insiders say that while Australians are worried about Hanson's attacks on multiculturalism, her criticism of Islam does resonate in broader parts of the community.

One Labor MP said he believed that Australians probably agreed with some of Hanson's views on Islam and conceded this was a political tightrope for Labor, as some voters see Muslims as the exception to the nation's multicultural story.

Pauline Hanson's momentum has been based on squeezing voter grievances on everyday issues and piling them on migration. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Hanson weaponises issue

Hanson's momentum has been based on squeezing voter grievances on everyday issues and piling them on migration, blaming Muslims in particular for Australia's housing and economic issues.

Last week she claimed that it was Muslims rorting the NDIS. Her effectiveness in weaponising this has made Labor more sensitive in how it not just speaks about the issue but manages it.

Albanese has not been seen visiting a mosque since March this year, when he was heckled in some ugly and uncomfortable scenes.

While this is a challenge for Labor, it is proving a splitting headache for the Coalition, not just because of Hanson, but also its own federal president, Tony Abbott.

Earlier in the week, the former PM appeared in a video declaring multiculturalism has failed and "diversity is indeed not our strength":

" Numerous Muslim leaders seem less interested in condemning that atrocity — the worst ever terrorist attack on our soil — and in chiding the public about the dangers of Islamophobia, even though there are some parts of Islamic thought that are hardly compatible with life in a liberal democracy. "

Appearing on Insiders yesterday morning, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg said he strongly disagreed with Abbott's views.

Loading...

The problem for the Liberal Party is Abbott is no longer freelancing as a former PM; his role as party president may be distinct from the Liberal shadow cabinet, but like Hanson, his voice carries weight.

His interventions on Islam and multiculturalism are at best a distraction for Bragg and his leader, Angus Taylor.

At worst, they make it harder for Taylor to have the clear air he needs to differentiate from Hanson and rebuild the Liberal supporter base.

Jane Hume, Angus Taylor and Tony Abbott have different takes on migration and multiculturalism. (AAP Image: Jay Kogler)

'They were divisive'

The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, also criticised Pauline Hanson for statements about migration and multiculturalism at the CPAC conference in London, telling Sky News Australia she condemns the One Nation leader's comments.

"I think that they were unnecessary. They were divisive. They were inflammatory, and they were totally un-Australian," Hume said.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

"That's not the way we operate in Australia. We have had a proud history of multiculturalism. We're a great migrant nation."

Hume said Hanson was wrong to lament the removal of the White Australia policy in the 1960s and 1970s. On this front, Hanson has tried to walk back the comments in a social media video, blaming the media for misconstruing what she said.

But it begs the obvious question: why did she mention its dismantling, and how is any of her rhetoric helpful in growing her vote rather than dampening her surge?

While some Liberal frontbenchers want to distance themselves from the extreme rhetoric against Muslims and multiculturalism, their party president has made that product differentiation much more difficult.

Loading

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: One telehealth consult and a doctor prescribed unapproved peptides
World.content:
The booming industry selling Australians on the promise of living longer and turning back the clock on aging is exploiting significant gaps in health regulation, exposing consumers to risk.

Four Corners has identified around 100 operators that have opened in Australia, offering services they say will keep you young, beautiful, strong and full of energy. They advertise IV drips, red light therapy, cryotherapy and hyperbaric chambers.

Clinics are offering NAD+ infusions to fire up your mitochondria, boost your energy and keep you younger for longer.

These treatments may look and sound medical. But for many of the anti-aging claims, the sales pitch has raced ahead of the evidence. For example, with NAD+, despite little evidence of benefit in humans, there are laboratory research findings that it has a role in cancer.

Some clinics sell customers red light therapy. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

And then there are peptides — short chains of protein building blocks called amino acids. While peptides such as insulin and GLP-1 agonists like Ozempic are part of mainstream medicine, the peptides in the anti-aging industry are unproven and unapproved.

Social media is awash with people unlawfully spruiking these injectables for everything from a hot body, glowing skin and shiny hair to an instant tan.

While many get them from overseas black-market manufacturers, some are turning to Australian doctors at wellness or longevity clinics.

To test how easy or hard it is to get a prescription, ABC health reporter Rachel Carbonell booked a "peptide therapy" consultation of her own.

Rachel's 'peptide therapy'

The website for the Queensland wellness clinic I booked with said peptide treatments were available to suitable patients, prescribed by the clinic doctor.

When I clicked on the link to book the appointment, I was directed to a long questionnaire about my health, then referred for a panel of blood tests, and I had to send through a health summary including any past scans or results.

Rachel Carbonell was given a telehealth appointment for a clinic's "peptide therapy". (Four Corners)

Once I had jumped through these hoops, which took a couple of weeks, I was offered a telephone consult. To secure an appointment, I first had to sign an informed consent form.

It said that I had been advised of alternatives, including lifestyle changes, approved treatments or no treatment at all. I wasn't sure where this advice was supposed to have come from given I hadn't yet seen a doctor.

By this time, I was about $400 down for the blood tests, a GP appointment for the health summary and the telehealth appointment fee.

I asked if we could do the consultation by video but was told the doctor only did them by telephone. She called me and started with a thorough run-through of my blood tests, previous scans and medical history.

When the doctor asked me what I booked the appointment for, I gave an honest description of what I assume is typical for many 50-something women. I'm feeling a bit old and fatigued; I often wake early in the morning and can't get back to sleep; building muscle at the gym is harder than it used to be; I have a sore lower back, and I've got a niggling hamstring injury.

I did say that I was looking for something anti-aging in nature and beyond the kinds of offerings I was receiving from my own GP.

Rachel was not asked what other options she had tried. (Four Corners)

At this point, the doctor acknowledged that "in Australia peptides are very controversial" and that they "should be a last resort" and must only be prescribed for a legitimate medical condition.

I had already mentioned my diet and exercise routine, my peri-menopause treatment and my home physio routine. We did not discuss what other options I had tried or not, or if I had seen other doctors and exhausted all other options. Instead, she said my legitimate medical conditions were my "degenerative issues" and potentially, insomnia.

The doctor then recommended one peptide to heal my hamstring and my "degeneration", another peptide for overall improvement in my skin and "aesthetics", and then another two for sleep and muscle repair.

A "stack", as they say, of four different unapproved peptides with little or no scientific evidence in people that they do the jobs they are promoted to do.

The doctor was forthright about the lack of data on the long-term safety of the peptides and mentioned that it was important that I had no pre-existing cancer risks.

Given that I live in Victoria and she was based in Queensland, I asked what to do if something went wrong. She said I should stop taking them and go to a doctor.

Rachel's treatment plan offered an option that would cost $1,181 for a four-to-six-week supply. (Four Corners)

I was sent a treatment proposal, which had only my first name on it, no doctor's name or signature. It appeared to be a generic form, outlining the risks and benefits of each product. It included options to have them compounded and packaged into an injection pen, costing $1,181 for a four-to-six-week supply.

The invoice note said once I had paid, the clinic would issue the prescription to the pharmacy and arrange dispensing and shipping.

A reality check

Four Corners gave Rachel's treatment plan to endocrinologist Katherine Samaras to review.

"To me it reads like a legal document that has been written to protect the company that is prescribing and dispensing [the peptides]," Professor Samaras said.

"Most of what I see in that report is really to protect the company rather than inform, guide and treat Rachel."

Katherine Samaras says the peptide prescription could have serious health risks. (Four Corners)

Professor Samaras said the recommendation for a follow-up blood test a month after starting the peptide treatment was a red flag because "anyone who knows their endocrinology knows that it takes three months to reach peak" levels induced by the growth hormone stimulating peptides.

She warned that some of the peptides prescribed come with known health risks because they stimulate growth factors.

"It'll have the muscle-boosting, muscle-building effects, but it will promote fluid retention, it will promote osteoarthritis, inflammation, deranged glucose metabolism and increased diabetes risk if she's a susceptible person,"

But Professor Samaras said the biggest potential risk was stimulating or promoting cancer.

"The big question for me is cancer; we know that they act on cancer pathways."

'Profits ahead of patients'

It may seem surprising that doctors can prescribe these unapproved peptides.

Unapproved does not necessarily mean unlawful, but it does mean they have not been assessed for safety, quality and effectiveness by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

There are regulations that allow for this in Australia, but they were designed for people with compelling clinical needs, not to provide routine access to products without an established therapeutic role.

Responsibility is divided between product and practitioner regulation. The TGA regulates therapeutic goods, while the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) and the relevant national boards oversee the doctors and pharmacists who prescribe and dispense them.

But wellness and longevity clinics appear to be taking advantage of the gaps in enforcement and regulations.

"There are allowances for doctors to make their own decisions backed up by robust evidence … to prescribe unapproved products to their patients," the TGA's chief medical advisor Professor Robyn Langham said.

"We don't regulate clinicians, that job is for AHPRA," Professor Langham said.

Health and longevity clinics appear to be taking advantage of the gaps in enforcement and regulations. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

AHPRA chief executive Justin Untersteiner said the regulator was "concerned that some practitioners may be seeking to exploit the latest health trends by putting profits ahead of patients".

"This is unacceptable. The onus is on practitioners to do the right thing and follow good practice, regardless of the business model," he said in a statement.

"AHPRA is limited in what it can say about individual matters but can confirm that we have open notifications regarding prescribing and supply of peptides."

He said good practice includes "only recommending treatments when there is an identified therapeutic need and a reasonable expectation of clinical efficacy and benefit for the patient."

AHPRA said it was being proactive, "not just responding to complaints", and had made clear the expectations around prescribing, compounding and telehealth.

There is no shortage of sites selling black market peptides. (Four Corners)

The TGA does regulate, and strictly forbids, advertising prescription or unapproved products.

When Four Corners asked the clinic that provided Rachel Carbonell with a prescription if its online offering of "peptide therapy" was legal, the clinic said it was because the website "did not advertise any specific prescription" and that "booking a consultation did not guarantee that any medicine would be prescribed".

It has since removed and renamed that particular service.

Professor Langham said the majority of the supply of unapproved peptides was happening via the black market, which the TGA is attempting to crack down on.

Four Corners had samples of three black market peptides sent to a Melbourne Lab for analysis.

Vials of GHK-CU, a copper peptide often promoted for skin and hair. (Four Corners: Patrick Stone)

It found the concentrations of the peptides varied widely. One sample contained none of the advertised peptide at all.

Grace Hamann, an analytical chemist, said the lab also found heavy metals in some peptide samples, including significant amounts of potentially toxic free copper.

"Generally, it's there as a marketing gimmick … to make the peptide in the vial appear blue," she said.

Professor Samaras said the longevity industry was capitalising on people's desire for better health.

"People are vulnerable. They're trying to do the right thing by their health, and they think that there is something more that they can add to it, but they have been utterly misled."

Watch Four Corners' full investigation The Race to Reverse Aging tonight from 8:30 on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: How can you get the balance right when being online is your job?
World.content:
As our reliance on smartphones and social media continues to grow, experts say it's getting harder to switch off, blurring the line between work and personal time.

And for people who need to be across social, news and industry trends for work, it can be particularly tricky.

"Where you're constantly monitoring … it's just harder to get respite from [work]," says Paula Brough, professor of organisational psychology and director of the Centre for Work, Organisation and Wellbeing at Griffith University in Brisbane/Meanjin.

" We know the evidence is clear that workers need that recovery period. "

AI solutions consultant Melissa Westbrook, a South Australian now living in London, feels the pull to keep up with industry developments.

"I'm so big on keeping up with AI trends," she says.

"What I think is challenging from a lifestyle perspective [is] … I spend a lot of time in front of screens throughout the day.

"For me, it's important to get that balance right between professional necessity and personal interests."

Melissa Westbrook now lives in the UK. (Supplied)

In Eora country/Sydney, coach, speaker and author Claire Baker feels the pressure, too.

Claire's business is centred around menstrual cycle awareness, and she runs online training for professionals who want to integrate it into their own work.

"My business is totally online and it's also very global," she says.

"Most of my clients and students are in the Northern Hemisphere … so it's like I could be working at all hours of the day. I think when you're running an online business, that's the reality for a lot of people."

Claire Baker's work is predominantly online. (Supplied: Hannah Jones)

Claire says while she's fairly good at setting boundaries between her work and personal life, striking a balance is still tough at times, particularly when it comes to using social media for work.

"It's such a great tool. But the problem is that it's so addictive … especially if you're following a lot of other business owners," she says.

" I find if I've been on there a lot — scrolling, looking at also what my peers are up to — [suddenly] it's like, oh God, I've just been watching ads for about an hour. "

Finding the line between work and play

Guruk/Port Macquarie psychologist Ernest Materyn works with clients suffering from symptoms of anxiety and depression often stemming from burnout at work.

He says for those doing highly online work, the real problem can be knowing what's work and what isn't.

Ernest Materyn says smartphones and internet have reshaped the way we work, and we're still catching up. (Supplied)

Your smartphone can mean work comes home in your pocket.

"Most work, historically, has a natural endpoint … the online world doesn't," he says.

"We are the first generation that is dealing with something for which there's no manual, there's no guide, and it [the internet] has completely … revolutionised the way we work.

"Social media keeps updating, the trend keeps moving, the conversation continues without you."

As a starting point, Mr Materyn recommends pausing before jumping on your phone after work and really considering what you're about to use it for.

"Ask yourself, 'What am I doing? Is this work or is this leisure?'" he says.

Paula Brough is a Meanjin/Brisbane-based professor of organisational psychology. (Supplied)

Professor Brough says occasionally bringing work home isn't a problem, but when it becomes a pattern, it can lead to burnout.

"If you only live and breathe work, that's a huge danger sign," she says.

"You need something else, whether it's sport or family or some other non-work activity."

Professor Brough says becoming irritable, thinking about conversations from work in your downtime and trouble sleeping are all signs to watch for.

"These are all these symptoms … [indicating,] 'OK, this is affecting my behaviour and my health. I need a break,'" she says.

Taking work home and staying "switched on" outside hours can become problematic, Paula Brough says. (Unsplash: Helena Lopes)

How to strike a balance

In Australia, there are laws protecting workers' rights to disconnect but sometimes, as with Melissa and Claire, work done at home isn't the result of direct pressure from a boss.

How to navigate your right to disconnect Experts share advice to help turn the the right to disconnect from principle to practice in your working life.

In this case, Professor Brough says setting clear boundaries for yourself is important.

"Time boundaries … I'm only working between X and Y and I'm not going to work, which includes checking emails on phones, in the evening or at weekends, for example," she says.

"There are also geographical boundaries. So, I'm only working when I'm sitting at my desk … and then when I leave that area, I turn into a non-worker."

Mr Materyn says behaviours that signal to your brain that work is over, such as changing clothes when you get home or going for a walk, are also helpful, as is being intentional about how you use your free time.

What balance can look like in real life

To maintain balance in her life, Melissa uses a routine she started during London's COVID lockdowns.

"At 6am, I'll go for a nice walk around where I live," Melissa says.

Melissa lives in London and makes a point of regularly getting out to explore the city. (Unsplash: Nick Page)

She then allocates time in her day for keeping up with trends in AI and her industry.

"I'll come back, do my prep work for my actual job, but that's also when I do my research, what's happening in the news, in AI … trends in the industry and so on," Melissa says.

"That makes me knowledgeable for the workday."

She's also intentional about spending quality time offline, going out with friends, socialising, hitting theatres and galleries, and exploring London.

"I'll make a real point of making my Saturday afternoons in particular really beneficial," she says.

" I try to go away on the weekends as much as possible … those are the sorts of things that can really add that variety into your life, so you don't feel like you're glued in front of a screen. "

Another way she has built balance into her life has been taking her quest for knowledge about her industry offline.

After attending a "no code and brew" session, Melissa is now involved as a speaker. (Supplied)

"I started attending these 'no code and brew' hackathon sessions [outside work] … and I brought some of my own AI skill building there," she says.

"From a wellness perspective … actually getting into a room, having a nice chat, maybe a few pizzas and some coffees, and just learning from each other … that's a real way to bring that work-life balance into the mix as well."

For Claire, boundary setting has been key to maintaining her work-life balance.

"I work from home, so … I don't work out of my bedroom, for example," she says.

As a general rule, she doesn't work after 6pm and she "fiercely" protects her days off.

Claire has built a business that doesn't rely on social media, which means she can take an extended break from scrolling when she needs to. (Supplied: Hannah Jones)

Claire also sets boundaries around social media, using desktop apps for work-related posts, which she says feel less "addictive" than her phone, and deleting social media apps every weekend.

"But sometimes I just need a month away," she says.

"I don't know if I'd recommend that as a business strategy, but it's been fine for me."

Only finding out their destination with a day's notice, each filmmaker had just 10 days to find a story and produce a short film, to be judged by a panel of experts.

Get to know the contestants

Mikaela Read more Describe yourself in three words: Artistic, poetic, magazine. My motto for Race Around the World is: Art is subjective. Not everyone is going to like your film, so as long as you make something that you're proud of, it doesn't really matter if people don't like it. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: Wired headphones. There's too much travel to rely on a charged set of AirPods. My greatest fear while overseas is: Having luggage go overboard and get wet. With all our filming gear, water is really hard to recover from. Elliot Read more Describe yourself in three words: Chaotic, introverted extrovert. My motto for Race Around the World is: I always liked this saying in Portuguese, "Viva como se fosse morrer amanhã", which is like, live as if you will die tomorrow. I think you just need to enjoy every day. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My glasses, but I'll lose them. I've lost three pairs of glasses in the last month. My greatest fear while overseas is: Something happening to people that I love while I'm away. Jayden Read more Describe yourself in three words: Easy-going, lively, passionate. My motto for Race Around the World is: I think this one's actually plagiarised from the big man David Attenborough, but if people don't care about something, they won't protect it, and people won't care about something they can't see. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My long lens. It's a really long, stupidly heavy, big thing that no one in their right mind would want to carry when you're running around to 10 different countries. My greatest fear while overseas is: Getting to day nine and a story having completely fallen through, or if I shot a full story with someone, and then I'm ready to submit it, and for whatever reason, the person in the story pulls the pin. Lucinda Read more Describe yourself in three words: Bubbly, curious, unconventional. My motto for Race Around the World is: YOLO [you only live once]. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: A necklace that means a lot to me, that's my talisman. My greatest fear while overseas is: The logistics. I dread not getting sleep. Kate Read more Describe yourself in three words: Curious, Wollongong, humorist My motto for Race Around the World is: Water off a duck's back. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My nan's ring, that would be my lucky charm. My greatest fear while overseas is: A misunderstanding would be really dreadful. Being Australian, I feel like we have a very good sense of humour, but it can also be a little bit different. You don't want people to think you're making fun of them, but that's sometimes how that can be interpreted. William Read more Describe yourself in three words: Content, introspective, disorganised My motto for Race Around the World is: Have fun. One item that's making the suitcase no matter what: My Nintendo Switch. My greatest fear while overseas is: My reputation for being a machine learning engineer getting tarnished by the fact that, I don't know, maybe I say something about not wanting to do it when really, I love my job.

World.title: Live: World Cup final pits Spain and Argentina for the ultimate prize
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Argentina will try to become the first team to defend a World Cup title since 1962 in the final on Sunday against a Spanish side that could boast the next generation's greatest player in Lamine Yamal.

The path to the afternoon kickoff in East Rutherford has been decidedly more emotional for Argentina, who twice came from behind and twice required extra time during the knockout phase.

That included two late goals assisted by the current generation's greatest player - 39-year-old Lionel Messi.

Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez scored in a dramatic 2-1 win over England in Wednesday's semifinal.

But manager Lionel Scaloni said the outbursts of emotions that have accompanied each win are exactly what is needed to process such a run, which may well be Messi's last.

It's also a reflection of the seismic support that has followed the Albiceleste to stadiums across the United States.

"We've recovered something which is extremely valuable, which is the fact that people are watching our games on TV, wearing the Argentinian jersey and hugging each other," Scaloni said. "This feeling of unity, we really feel it. People are with us, supporting us and backing us. And that's very emotional for us. And it's good to express emotions. I believe that's part of life. It's part of what we are. And that makes you even more human."

After winning Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024 with Argentina, Messi is attempting to help his homeland become the third back-to-back World Cup champion, following Italy in 1934 and 1938, and Pelé's Brazil in 1958 and 1962.

Meanwhile, his teammates have been trying to embrace the moment, a luxury they didn't have in 2022 when they shouldered the pressure of ending a 36-year World Cup drought.

"I am enjoying this World Cup much more than the one in Qatar," admitted 33-year-old goalkeeper Emi Martínez. "And for me, being in my fifth final with a national team, well, I don't want to take credit away from me. "I am eternally thankful to my teammates, and I just want to enjoy. I'm going to jump on the pitch with a smile, as this is something that many players cannot achieve."

World.title: As a backpacker, Martin changed my life. We found each other again 30 years later
World.content:
InspirationEurope As a backpacker, Martin changed my life. We found each other again 30 years later Kate Armstrong July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last thing I expect when I walk into Berlin’s Hotel Adlon Kempinski is to burst into tears. My suite overlooks Pariser Platz and the Brandenburg Gate. Built by the Prussians, this neoclassical monument – topped by Victory steering her chariot drawn by four horses – is now a powerful symbol of Germany’s reunification in 1990. I’m not weeping at the scene (which is beautiful), but for the reason I’m here. I visited Berlin as a young backpacker with my friend Caroline, four months after the fall of the Berlin Wall. The wall had not yet been dismantled, which meant we still had to go through Checkpoint Charlie – what had been the border crossing between the American sector and Soviet-controlled East Berlin – and change Deutschmarks to the near-worthless East German Ostmarks. I vaguely recall the border post’s long, rectangular building. Behind a narrow, brown counter a uniformed guard placed a small slip of paper – not an official rubber stamp – into our passports. Berlin Cathedral, on the capital’s Museum Island and Spree River at sunset. Getty Images On entering the East, and with no plans, we wandered aimlessly up Friedrichstrasse until we reached Unter den Linden, a wide boulevard lined with crumbling grand mansions. Here, we lucked upon a handsome baroque building, Humboldt University, it transpired. Students around our age were pouring out of its massive iron gates. Keen to engage, we asked if anyone spoke English. A young man, his thick hair tied back in a ponytail, introduced himself as Martin. This exchange would change my life. On learning we were Australian, Martin jumped: he invited us to his English class. (“We hadn’t heard any native English speakers until then,” he explained later.) Thrilled, if a little nervous, we agreed. The class fired questions at us, mainly about our travels; until then, their travels had been restricted to Eastern Bloc countries.



After class, Martin approached us, four others in tow: “Come, we’d like to show you our East Berlin.” This six-hour jaunt was the beginning of many journeys together, including, several months later, a backpacking trip through Portugal. Given our new friends’ lack of funds, our group travelled on a shoestring: we ate market produce, camped illegally on beaches, and caught the cheaper, slow trains. It was magical. Free from their experiences under a repressive regime, they willingly reflected on the impact of the Stasi, the East German secret police. 



Out of nowhere, 30 years since our last contact, Martin tracked me down. And one year later, here I am. Back in Berlin. Our reunion at Hotel Adlon Kempinski is easy, the conversation seamless. The “whys” are left well alone. For now, at least. First, we’ll retrace our first steps through the former East Berlin. But as we start to explore, I become confused. My mind oscillates wildly between the past and the present, like a tune that loses its groove on a scratched vinyl LP and can’t regain traction. While I’m able to square this gentle, middle-aged man with the intense, athletic youth I first knew, I can’t yet reconcile the Berlin of my former experience with the city before me. I’m as hazy as the smog that used to hang over the East, the legacy of the brown coal that the “Ossis” (East Germans) burned in their fireplaces and stoves. Checkpoint Charlie, once a famous crossing point on the border of West and East Berlin during the Cold War. Getty Images The one exception is Humboldt University, where we first met. I recognise it immediately. This handsome stone baroque building remains much as it was, though it’s cleaner now, the grey exterior having been scrubbed of layers of grime. Inside the university’s airy lobby, the lingering aroma of disinfectant transports me back to Caroline whispering under her breath, “It smells like a hospital.” Back on Unter den Linden, Mercedes-Benz and other slick European cars stream past. They’re a far cry from the “Trabis”, the tiny Trabant vehicles that I recall putt-putting by, their two-stroke engines spewing sour, noxious fumes. Just beyond the university is Museum Island, a small section of land surrounded by the River Spree. We recreate our tour of all those years ago. We pose against the backdrop of the Berlin Cathedral. We climb to the top of the Französischer Dom (French Cathedral) and peer across at the Concert House and German Church. Beyond these, the cityscape is unfamiliar to me.



We wander northwest, to the historic Jewish Quarter. My yesteryear photos depict blackened buildings, pocked with bullet marks – the legacy of World War II – and piles of furniture covering the footpaths, the discards of squatters who’d moved into buildings following reunification. Today, it’s another world; even the Neue Synagogue has had a glorious makeover. The surrounding streets feature leafy courtyards, trendy restaurants, design offices and yoga studios (though scars remain; bullet marks are prolific in places). A section of the Berlin Wall is a reminder that the city and its visitors are never far from history. Getty Images As for Prenzlauer Berg, an inner-city neighbourhood, where Martin himself had “claimed” an apartment all those years ago? Gone are the grey hues, the crumbling walls, the boarded-up windows. Related Article Germany Seven highlights you need to see at Berlin’s notorious wall The decay has been eradicated. Instead, digital nomads sit in the shade outside cafes, design boutiques sit alongside bookshops and stylish, multi-storey buildings have replaced those mansions that were too dilapidated to be repaired. It’s vibrant, colourful and welcoming. Our last stop, Potsdamer Platz, is seared in my mind. I recall the Berlin Wall behind a vast void, not the buzzy commercial centre before me. A subtle line of stone blocks delineates where the wall once ran. I’m disoriented, but amazed by the transformation.



On my final evening, I present Martin with a collection of photos from our time in Berlin and our former travels together. We reminisce about the group, long since splintered. Martin is no longer in touch with Stefan, his “radical” best friend. After reunification, Stefan left Germany and cut off all former ties; it turns out his parents were full-time, paid officials of the Stasi, part of the regime he so vehemently opposed. Street life in Prenzlauer Berg, once home to boarded-up windows, now one of Berlin’s best addresses. Getty Images The Berlin city skyline with views over Tiergarten park to the Brandenburg Gate, cathedral and the so-called “red city hall”. iStock I’m sad for Stefan, but hardly surprised. So much has been written about the former Eastern bloc, including Stasiland, Australian author Anna Funder’s captivating and award-winning book. Published in 2003, it reveals much about individuals’ lives in the former German Democratic Republic. Stefan’s story is typical of so many who bear past traumas. So now is the time to hear why Martin had been silent for so long. What reason, what secret, does he have for his estrangement? I hold my breath. It’s remarkably straightforward. So mundane that I immediately write myself “out” of a Stasiland sequel. It has nothing to do with the Stasi. Nor enigmas. But simply, a former partner unable to embrace Martin’s life before they were a couple. And, in his words, Martin’s inability to handle this maturely. Now, happily re-partnered, he is reconnecting with his past. And that includes me.



So, here we are, sipping on champagne in the stunning Hotel Adlon Kempinski. It’s an appropriate place to reunite. Built in 1907, the hotel was the height of opulence during the “Golden Years” between the world wars. It partly burned down during World War II and was later demolished. After reunification, it was rebuilt in a way to reflect the hotel’s traditional design, heritage and soul. Related Article Opinion

My happy place This city became my favourite place in the world, once they got rid of the guns Ute Junker Travel writer New but old. Old but new. Just like our friendship. And the revitalised, ever-changing, German capital. Kate Armstrong was a guest of Hotel Adlon Kempinski.
