World.title: Australians love Bali, Thailand and Vietnam. Why do we ignore this gem?
World.content:
InspirationMalaysia Australians love Bali, Thailand and Vietnam. Why do we ignore this gem? James Manning July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians love Asia, and rightly so. From Bali to Bangkok and Hokkaido to Hanoi, there is an abundance of fantastic food and culture in our corner of the world. But one tropical paradise that is practically on our doorstep is often overlooked. Why do we ignore Malaysia? In the 12 months up to May this year, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Australians took roughly twice as many trips to Thailand and Vietnam, and five times as many trips to Indonesia, as they did to Malaysia. Whether you’re in the market for a well-earned rest from the chaos of modern life – think White Lotus vibes without breaking the bank – or a short stopover in Kuala Lumpur on the way to Europe, this country has a lot to offer. Here’s how to make it work for you. Tanjong Jara Resort by YTL Hotels on the east coast of Malaysia. The beach resort



From KL, take a one-hour flight to Kuala Terengganu on the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia. There’s no shortage of budget accommodation around the city, but my destination is a boutique resort about an hour south, near Kuala Dungun. 



If you’re game, you can even go snorkelling or scuba diving with whale sharks off the nearby Tenggol island (September is the best time of year to spot them). For something more passive, you can watch fireflies dance in the dark on an evening cruise up the Dungun River, just be sure to wear plenty of insect repellent and avoid wearing black (it attracts mosquitoes). For something more hands-on, visit the on-site turtle hatchery, which has rescued and relocated more than 100,000 eggs from potential poachers since 2016 (the eggs are still hunted and sold on the black market despite scientists debunking the myth that eating them can cure asthma). The numbers sound immense, but only one in 1000 hatchlings makes it to adulthood in the wild. As well as being hunted by reef sharks, ghost crabs, monitor lizards, and seabirds, juvenile turtles have to contend with ocean plastic and fishing trawler nets. This means as few as 100 adults may have survived as a result of this program, showing why many species remain critically endangered and highlighting the importance of the work. If you’re staying at the resort during nesting or hatching season (April through October) you can even opt in to receive a call in the middle of the night to help out. The rooms are superb, but it’s hard to stay indoors when the surrounding nature is so beautiful.



If not, you can laze by one of the two pools or enjoy a variety of treatments at the spa. I opt for the traditional Malay, which begins with a floral bath followed by a deep tissue massage with herbal oils, ginger and galangal to improve blood circulation. Beforehand, a form asks me if I want to leave energised, relaxed, stress-free, headache-free or with clearer skin. There is no “all of the above” option, but I tick every box nonetheless. I needn’t have worried, the masseuse, Aida, is a master with her hands. The next day I visit the nearby Dungun Market – home to endless stalls of fresh seafood, satay jellyfish, dried chillies, pickled lychees, and more herbs than I ever knew existed – before returning to the resort for a cooking class. We learn how to make the perfect beef rendang and coconut curry with prawns (tofu is available for vegetarians). The secret, it turns out, is palm sugar, also known as “Malaysian candy”. Traditional Malay-inspired lobby area at Tanjong Jara Resort. The food here, whether cooked by yourself or the staff, is a highlight. “People come here to heal and eat well,” says chef Ann, a larger-than-life character who has been working here for more than 20 years.



The sambal chilli sauce at the breakfast buffet is one of the best I’ve ever tasted. The only thing more addictive is the endless warmth and hospitality of the staff, all of whom seem genuinely happy to help guests with anything and everything. “My job is half job and half holiday,” says rooms manager Jazz Jusoh, only half-jokingly. Before checking out, more than once I seriously consider applying for a job and staying. The iconic twin spires of Kuala Lumpur’s Petronas Towers. iStock The city break If you’re in need of a pit stop on the way to Europe, Kuala Lumpur has a lot to offer, especially if you’ve already done Singapore and Hong Kong. “KL never sleeps,” a local cheerily informs me soon after I arrive, and many here seem to follow that maxim to a tee. You can shop ’til you drop at Pavilion or Suria mall, before checking out the view upstairs from the top of the Petronas Twin Towers (the world’s tallest building from 1996 to 2004).



For a more unique cultural experience (one with shops you won’t find in every other world city), check out the stalls at Central Market and the nearby Petaling Street Market. Or get out of the city on a day trip to visit the world-famous Batu Caves. At dinner time, head down to the Jalan Alor night market for freshly made nasi lemak, rendang, laksa, and – if you’re brave enough – durian. It’s not for me, but you do you. Lavantha cocktail bar in Kuala Lumpur. My night ends at Lavantha cocktail bar, an offshoot of the award-winning Penrose. Housed underground in what was previously a bank vault, it’s run by three friends, one of whom studied in Melbourne. The menu is full of modern twists on classics, and I opt for the blueberry Gibson, which adds blueberries, thyme and white balsamic vinegar to gin with refreshing results. It goes down well with the small plates on offer, including potato terrine with a miso yuzu emulsion and smoked salmon aguachile. Someone suggests kicking on to the nightclub Over and Above (apparently the place to be seen) but unlike KL, I do need to sleep and I call it a night. An island adventure on the west coast beckons.



Sea villas at Pangkor Laut Resort, off the west coast of Malaysia. The private island There are a lot more Malaysian islands beyond Penang and Langkawi. In fact, there are more than 800. So if it’s island living you crave, head north from KL up the west coast for about three hours to the state of Perak. From here, you can transfer to a private oasis. To arrive on Pangkor Laut by speedboat is to get a glimpse of how the other half live. There are 140 villas spread across this 120-hectare island, 43 of which are on stilts over water. There are two pools to choose from, but the best place to relax here is the spa village, a title it definitely earns – the place is enormous. Treatments start with a Chinese-style foot massage before men and women are separated for a three-part bathing experience.



The bath house at Pangkor Laut’s spa village. First up is a refreshing cold water pool, where you can be gently massaged by a series of waterfalls before unwinding in a hot Japanese-style onsen with a cup of ice-cold green tea. Finally, a full-body exfoliation before being led to a private villa for a 90-minute campur-campur treatment, which mixes traditional Malay and Thai massage. Every part of it is blissful, and I’d return to the spa every day if time and money allowed. If you feel inspired to continue your wellness journey, yoga classes are held in the mornings by the sea in a villa that also hosts operas once a year, inspired by a former guest, Italian tenor Luciano Pavarotti. Related Article Asia Asia’s 25 greatest cities to visit, ranked and rated Later, I catch a buggy to the private beach, and I’m nursing a cocktail while lazing in a hammock outside Chapman’s Bar. It’s named after British Colonel Freddy Chapman, who hid on the island from the Japanese during World War II before making a daring escape by swimming out to a British submarine.



Unlike competitors in the annual Chapman’s Challenge, I don’t attempt to recreate this feat, but I do indulge in a dip. The water is warm here (though not quite the perfection I enjoyed on the east coast). Plastic pollution is a problem due to recent storms so men with rakes and wheelbarrows do what they can. It’s like having your own private beach at Pangkor Laut Resort. It’s not the only environmental effort on this island, where endangered hornbills and flying foxes thrive. The conservation team also rehabilitate turtles that have swallowed plastic and can no longer dive to get food because they are too buoyant. There are even critically endangered pangolins here, although they’re incredibly rare. We don’t spot any, and I can’t help but feel the less human contact they have, the better. There are already long-tailed macaques on this island, and next year there are plans afoot to reintroduce another primate, the slow loris. “People say it’s futile but you have to try,” says the resort’s resident naturalist Aris. “I want to leave something for my kids.”

World.title: The rise and fall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime The rise and fall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family Riley Walter July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For gangland police, years of work had been leading to one day; they had intercepted phone calls, listened to conversations, surveilled targets and slowly but surely built briefs of evidence on Sydney’s underworld powerbrokers. In the early hours of a Wednesday morning, a little over two years ago, they moved in – 250 officers across the city’s south-west pounced in one of the most significant operations carried out by anti-gang police. Their targets – alleged senior members of the Alameddine organised crime network. By then, many of its highest-ranking members, including patriarch Rafat Alameddine, had fled the country for the safety of the Middle East. Left behind was a criminal syndicate estimated to be making $1 million a week from a sprawling drug trafficking empire. As the Alameddine family’s grip on the city’s lucrative drug trade increased, so too did the efforts of detectives on its tail. Finally, after years of pursuing the network’s upper echelons, they had broken through. The Alameddine organised crime network remains in Sydney in name only, police say. Aresna Villanueva



Having rounded up 16 people, including the family’s alleged local leader, Ali Elmoubayed, the message was clear: the Alameddine network’s Australian operations were all but finished, the infamous group had been eradicated, NSW Police Deputy Commissioner Dave Hudson said in March 2024. To the network’s puppet-masters abroad, the arrests signalled authorities’ focus despite their relocation. To the Alameddines’ underworld rivals, it signalled a shift in Sydney’s criminal landscape; no longer did the Merrylands clan rule the roost. The city was up for grabs. So swift has the downfall of Sydney’s most notorious crime family been since that senior police regard the Alameddine network as remaining in name only. As its once-feared enforcers have fled, been jailed or killed, its long-held grasp of the city’s illicit drug market has weakened. With a lack of local leadership, the struggle for a seat atop Sydney’s underworld has become a free-for-all; even the family’s most loyal followers have abandoned their allegiances to cash in on the city’s insatiable appetite for cocaine and methamphetamine. Members of KVT – a street gang comprising predominantly men of Fijian descent and long used by the Alameddine network as muscle – cut ties with their one-time allies during a mass exodus of powerbrokers from the crime family. Now, up against a contingent of turncoats and underworld upstarts, remaining members of the Alameddine network have become a hunted species. Rafat Alameddine, pictured in 2019, left Australia amid increased police scrutiny. Kate Geraghty



In January, the self-proclaimed Coconut Cartel firebombed the western Sydney home of Rafat Alameddine’s cousin, Bilal Alameddine. The cartel, comprising defected Alameddine network members and others vying for control of Sydney’s underbelly, vowed to “chalk out” any loyalists still flying the family’s flag; a line was drawn in the sand and war declared. The attacks since have been unrelenting and unwavering. In April, Rafat Alameddine’s vacant Merrylands home was peppered with bullets in a drive-by shooting, while homes and businesses linked to his brother-in-law, Asaad Alahmad, were targeted. Alahmad has been jailed for his involvement in Ready 4 War, the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation. The Coconut Cartel, which has rebranded several times in the past year, has claimed responsibility for the attacks under several gang names spruiked to gain notoriety. One, the so-called “Lone Wolves”, took the credit for several incidents in Sydney targeting the Alameddine network’s offshore leadership. The group, through video of their attacks and communications shared with burgeoning social media channel SCN Worldstar, promised an ever-increasing assault on the network. Day by day, the group said after claiming credit for an arson attack in April, it would drive the Alameddine network out of Sydney with the help of insiders willing to share the syndicate’s secrets. Another group believed to comprise alleged Coconut Cartel associates and members – dubbed the OC Jail Gang – also pledged its support to “eradicate” the Alameddines.





Closer to home, one of the last remaining alleged high-profile members of the network left on Sydney’s streets, the rapper “Ay Huncho”, recently heeded years of police warnings and left NSW after several threats to his life, including what detectives say was a foiled attempt to assassinate him in April. After a group of masked men allegedly kidnapped and beat his bodyguard in a late-night ambush, the rapper, whose legal name is Ali Younes, finally made himself scarce, relocating interstate. In May, Elmoubayed’s home was peppered with bullets as the 33-year-old languishes in custody, having been charged in December with plotting to murder a former ally, whose defection from the Alameddine network was the catalyst for months of tit-for-tat shootings and assassination attempts. Whatever their title, the groups targeting the Alameddine network have a common goal: seizing control of the underworld from its long-time rulers. “What we’re seeing now involves competing groups, shifting alliances and external actors trying to assert control,” Cook says. “These are loose, opportunistic networks with no hierarchy, no discipline and no long‑term loyalty. That lack of structure is one of the reasons conflicts escalate so quickly.” For police investigating the increased targeting of the Alameddine network, the blurred lines of the family’s rivals and the shifting criminal landscape present an increasingly challenging task; in a world where loyalty was a criminal’s most valuable asset, it is now a tradeable commodity. “The reality is that contract criminals move between groups, sometimes working for both sides of a conflict,” Cook says.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Drug kingpin’s suspected links to Vietnam assassination of Sydney cartel leader Recent drug seizures indicate South-East Asian organised crime groups have all but taken control of Sydney’s underworld from the Alameddine family. Overseas-based alleged kingpins, including former Sydney man Daniel Rodney Badger, have become the focus of detectives investigating the flow of drugs into Australia as criminal organisations band together to control the manufacture and supply of cocaine, methamphetamine and heroin. “When we dismantle one group, others step in to take the work and then we target them,” Cook says. “It’s a cycle we’re very familiar with.” Despite the distance between those police believe are pulling the strings abroad and the violence on Sydney’s streets, apprehending overseas-based organised crime figures is one of NSW Police’s highest priorities. “They hide behind foreign jurisdictions and encrypted platforms, but they are not out of reach,” Cook says. “When opportunities arise, we act. It may take time, but we don’t lose sight of them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: People think my suburb is posh, but it’s friendly and diverse – and I got my unit cheap
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion People think my suburb is posh, but it’s friendly and diverse – and I got my unit cheap Kellie Williams Contributor July 20, 2026 — 5:00am

July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When someone asks where I live and I say Ascot, the standard response is: “Ooh, fancy!” Yet I’m not rich, and I’ve never encountered snobbery here. Indeed, I’ve been regularly impressed by local shop owners who remember you by name from the first time you chat to them I have neighbours who are friendly and caring, not in an intrusive way, but genuinely look out for each other – like texting if I’ve accidentally left my garage door open, or picking up a package that’s been left in a weird spot by a delivery guy. On one occasion when I was sick, they’ve even offered to pick up groceries. There’s really no such thing as a typical Ascot person, just like there’s no such thing as a typical style of home in Ascot.



You know the place: that hilly suburb, landlocked by Albion, Clayfield, Hamilton and Hendra, a stone’s throw from the Brisbane River, the river you can easily see from so many vantage points in Ascot, from the hilltops to Kingsford Smith Drive. Named, obviously, after Ascot in England, hub of thoroughbred racing, our Ascot has long been a place for the betting on the nags, with Doomben and Eagle Farm Racecourse both taking up real estate here (and Albion Park just over the border). Ascot also has exceptional heritage houses such as Nyrambla, built in 1885. This one is especially interesting. It was requisitioned by the Allies in 1942 as a top-secret facility and used as a US-Australian intelligence base for codebreakers for three years – a Brisbane Bletchley Park. In the years since there have been several famous inhabitants, including ABC presenter Blair Edmonds, markets operator Jan Power, and beloved Queensland actor Bille Brown. As well as mansions, Ascot has art deco apartment buildings, Queenslander houses both updated and unrenovated, and daggy, rectangular unit blocks built between the 1960s and 1990s, giving it a very mixed aesthetic. There are big parks with towering trees, and local retail gems, such as the super-convenient IGA Marketplace at Oriel Park and the RSPCA Op Shop, full of quality finds, plus a variety of restaurants and cafes.



Inhabitants benefit from close access to great neighbours: Hamilton’s Eat Street Northshore, New Farm’s Powerhouse and James Street precinct, Newstead’s Bunnings, the Valley’s Homemaker, Albion’s Fonzie Abbott, Thai Ways and Bathhouse, and Clayfield’s convenient shops along Sandgate Road. We are also close to the airport, but I’ve never once heard a plane fly over. I’m a Sydneysider who lived in Cairns for a decade before moving to Brisbane in 2017. I had been renting across the inner south, inner east and inner west of Brisbane for six years when, as a middle-aged empty-nester happily enjoying my career and social life, I decided Brisbane was the best city in Australia to live in permanently, and was ready to purchase a property. Art deco apartment blocks on Lapraik Street. Markus Lavik This personal decision coincided with Brisbane’s COVID-induced property boom, and I was seeing prices increase steeply and steadily over the six months I was hunting. I was looking in the lower end of Brisbane’s price range, but wanted to be within a five-kilometre radius of the city. My biggest wishlist item was a private courtyard for my dogs and plants. To my surprise I just happened to find that in an Ascot unit. It was the second-cheapest one-bedroom unit I could find for sale in Brisbane when I bought it in mid-2023, and though it’s doubled in value in three years, it’s still one of the cheapest properties, and a very good investment. For that, I am grateful.



Though I moved to Ascot for the entry price and leafy courtyard, I quickly realised how lucky I was to live in such a pleasant and convenient suburb where it takes me no more than 15 minutes to get to the airport, the Valley, the city, two major hospitals, Westfield Chermside and even South Brisbane areas where I spend a lot of time socially. Related Article Public Transport We spent the morning at Brisbane’s loneliest train station Despite my preference for living close to town, I value having green spaces and nature close by. In my courtyard and neighbouring yards, I see owls, possums, lizards, pythons, bush turkeys and other birds, and did I mention lots of big trees? If I’m seeking an even quieter reprieve, just 20 minutes up the freeway I can relax at Sandgate and Brighton’s beautiful foreshore strips. Are we posh? Maybe some of the local schools are, and whoever’s living inside those grand mansions. But we’re a diverse suburb, with a warm, welcoming and safe community vibe.

World.title: Packed with roasted vegies and grains, these prep-ahead salads are built for winter
World.content:
Upgrade your cool-weather cooking with satisfying bowls that work for quick lunches, wholesome dinners or your next family gathering.

I absolutely love a good salad, but even I’ll admit that in the dead of winter, a bowl of cold lettuce isn’t going to cut it.

This is the time of year I start making salads that feel like a proper, hearty meal. By packing them with grains, lentils, chickpeas and roasted vegies, you get loads of texture and big flavours while still keeping things fresh and vibrant.

These are the kinds of salads I have on high rotation throughout winter. They’re perfect for prepping ahead for weekday lunches, pairing with your favourite protein for dinner, or bringing to a barbecue or family gathering when you’re asked to “just bring a salad”.

Best of all, they’re just as delicious served warm or at room temperature, making them incredibly versatile throughout the cooler months.

I hope they inspire you to think a little differently about winter salads because they really can be among the most satisfying meals you’ll make.

World.title: The 18 important medicines that Australians are missing out on
World.content:
PoliticsFederalMedicine The 18 important medicines that Australians are missing out on Natassia Chrysanthos July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just a quarter of new medicines launched globally in the last decade have been subsidised in Australia, putting life-changing treatments out-of-reach for patients, in a situation that pharmaceutical companies warn is becoming untenable. Eighteen key innovative treatments for cancer, mental illness, cardiology, immunology, rare diseases and infectious disease that are transforming people’s lives overseas are not available under Australia’s Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS). Medicines Australia, the peak pharmaceutical industry body, says local patients are missing out because of a complex and lengthy approvals process that is turning off drug companies, as the Trump administration stokes global pricing pressures. “The Australian market is no longer commercially attractive, or in some cases viable,” the lobby group says in a new report. “Australia’s low willingness to pay for innovative medicines has weakened the incentives for global pharmaceutical companies to launch new therapies in Australia.”



Editor's pick Political leadership Albanese once took on his own frontbench. Now he’s in charge, that would never happen Unavailable drugs include the first new schizophrenia treatment in a generation, and new interventions for narcolepsy, advanced prostate cancer and idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH). ‘It’s a job just to leave the house’ For 26 years Tina Powney, of Shepparton, Victoria, has lived with IPAH – a rare disease characterised by high blood pressure in the lung’s arteries – and is regularly out of breath and fatigued. Her treatment involves a continuous IV infusion connected to a catheter on her heart, controlled by a specialised pump she must wear in a band around her chest, 24 hours a day. Powney has had to go to hospital in Melbourne several times in the last six months to get new lines in, a 2.5-hour drive from home. She carries a bag containing medication and back-up pumps all the time, in case something fails.



Tina Powney finds it difficult to leave the house because of the amount of medicine and equipment she must carry at one time. A drug that could change that is not available in Australia yet. “I have a whole bedroom that’s just medication. To go on holidays is to fill the whole car with suitcases, dressings. You can’t just go down to the supermarket – you have to pack a backpack with everything. It’s a job just to leave the house, to visit a friend,” Powney said. A new drug, Sotatercept, was approved in the US and European Union in 2024. “It would require an injection every three weeks and that’s it,” Powney said. “It would change my whole life. I’d be able to go for a swim, go camping with my family, enjoy life like everyone else.” But it’s not on the PBS, under which the government subsidises drugs, so they cost Medicare cardholders $25 per script at most. Sotatercept’s out-of-pocket cost is about $16,000 – a sum that makes it inaccessible for Powney. The chief executive of Medicines Australia, Elizabeth de Somer, said it was cases like Powney’s that showed Australia had gone from a leader to laggard in funding new medicines.



“The real number of missing medicines is likely to be much, much higher, but these 18 medicines should be all the proof anyone needs that health standards in Australia are slipping and that is due to one thing – chronic underinvestment in the PBS,” she said. “I think if the public knew just how many innovative medicines are now bypassing Australia because of an outdated process, they would be justifiably alarmed. “This is not a hypothetical any more. It is a bitter pill to swallow for patients with schizophrenia, prostate cancer, Crohn’s disease and rare conditions who are missing out on treatments already helping people elsewhere.” According to the industry group’s analysis, investment in innovative medicines has fallen from 6.2 per cent to 4.1 per cent of the health budget since 2015-16. Over the same period, the likelihood a new medicine is reimbursed in Australia within two years’ approval in the US has dropped from 20 to 10 per cent. A McKell Institute survey this year found 43 per cent of Australians had been prescribed a medicine not on the PBS, and 29 per cent had to pay for a non-listed medicine in the last three years.



Why there are long delays in approvals Delays are often due to Australia’s process for approving and subsidising drugs. The Australian government negotiates cheaper prices by buying medicines in bulk, but the method for assessing cost-effectiveness means a new medicine cannot be more expensive than its lowest-priced competitor, unless it is proven to be significantly safer or better. Related Article Exclusive

Medical Malfunctions ‘Race to the bottom’: Investigation reveals toll of weak medical device laws It means it is harder for new medicines to compete against old versions that have become extremely cheap over time. Nor does it necessarily account for innovation – such as when a tablet replaces an injection, or small improvements to side effects that may improve the patient experience. This leads to long delays in approvals as drug companies and the government go back and forth gathering sufficient evidence – sometimes taking years.



Health Minister Mark Butler commissioned a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) review of these processes in 2022. In May 2024, it gave him 50 recommendations to speed up approvals and improve reimbursement pathways. These are currently being reviewed. But industry argues the task has been made more urgent as the Trump administration tries to bring medicine prices down in the US with a “most favoured nation” policy, which pushes drug companies to sell to the US at the lowest prices they sell at overseas. The risk is that manufacturers then avoid launching their products in smaller and lower-priced markets, such as Australia, so that they do not set a lower global baseline price. Butler has acknowledged that the US, and also China, were driving change in the medicines pricing. “We know patients want faster access to cutting-edge medicine and treatments. I recently met with 80 patient and consumer representatives to get their feedback on HTA, and I will continue to work with patients and industry to drive these reforms forward,” the minister said. “Work has been completed or is underway in response to number of the recommendations. Many of the HTA recommendations will be responded too as part of the strategic agreement with the medicines industry.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Social media is still white-hot on youth crime – just ask the police
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Social media is still white-hot on youth crime – just ask the police Matt Dennien July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland police have been measuring community views on youth crime through public sources such as social media, with a recent internal report giving an “extremely negative” score of just two out of 10. The one-page February document, obtained by this masthead, notes low confidence in bail and sentencing, “slogan heavy” fixes, fear-based narratives, polarisation on solutions, and “widespread distrust” of data. It comes as the Crisafulli LNP push ahead with its latest promised “circuit-breaker sentencing” program, and police and government spruik a new selective comparison of statistics. As the Crisafulli LNP government gears up for its next major push to meet election vows and toughen youth justice laws, an internal police report lays bare the task ahead. Michael Howard While partially tabled in parliament by the Labor Opposition last month, this masthead has since obtained the full Community Sentiment regarding the issue of Youth Crime – February 2026 document.



In a statement, a police spokesperson confirmed the agency monitored community sentiment through public information such as social media to “stay informed about key issues affecting Queenslanders”. “An internal report on youth crime sentiment was prepared to provide anecdotal insights,” the spokesperson said. “The information contained within it reflects community commentary and sentiment and should not be considered verified QPS data, intelligence, or an official measure of crime trends or community opinion.” In a section titled “summary of analysis”, an overall youth crime sentiment score of 2.1 out of 10 is given, described as “extremely negative”. A further breakdown shows 90 per cent leaned negative.



Key findings based on a “review of comments in response to youth crime coverage in the media” note the judiciary is blamed more than police, and people believe victim numbers are artificially reduced. Primary drivers of the comments are described as new law announcements, localised crime coverage, high profile political posts, and media coverage around enforcement or rehabilitation. Notable patterns in the comments include calls for mandatory sentencing and the removal of judicial discretion, and advocacy for the “castle law” pushed by Katter’s Australian Party. Support for structured rehabilitation programs, and recognition that poverty and trauma drive offending were also noted.



In the breakdown by police districts, sentiment in Townsville is described as the reference point for the “collapse” statewide, with the far north combining crime fear with political resentment, “making it more volatile”. In the south-east, negative sentiment in Logan is described as “less explosive”, but deeply entrenched, “making reassurance messaging difficult”. The Gold Coast, while not out of control, is “primed for escalation” with a major incident. Police refused to answer questions about whether the community sentiment work was ongoing, if such reports were being prepared regularly, and exactly what public information was used to inform it. Police also declined to say if the sentiment score or other elements had changed across any report updates, or if it had been presented to the government or Police Minister Dan Purdie – who refused to answer questions.





Speaking in Cairns with interim Police Commissioner Brett Pointing on Thursday, Crisafulli touted new police data showing victim numbers, robberies, unlawful entry and vehicle thefts had all fallen by 9.6, 19.5, 5 and 17.2 per cent, respectively. But this twice-yearly update from police was presented only as a comparison between the 2025-26 financial year and the 2023-24 financial year, the last of the former government, despite previously having been a comparison to the past 12 months. Police on Friday were unable to provide figures for the year-on-year change between 2024-25 and 2025-26. A spokesperson said 2023-24 had been picked as a reference point for a “baseline to assess changes over time” rather than a single year. Asked on Friday why the comparison had skipped a year, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie told reporters on the Sunshine Coast: “I think it is a pretty important statistic to show how bad it was under the Labor government, and it is getting better under our government.”



Recent independent state and federal data releases have shown victim numbers continuing to track downward since before the election, despite increasing rates for some crimes. On Thursday, Crisafulli repeated claims victim numbers had jumped 193 per cent in the past decade. Related Article Updated

Queensland budget Miles eyes crime data, housing and transport costs in new policies “There’s a reason why I’ve chosen to do this here in Cairns today,” Crisafulli said. “I’ve listened to the community. I’ve reflected on the levels of pain and frustration from the community. “In the last 10 years, victim numbers have increased by 193 per cent ... Now, any change that sees that not just stabilise, but come down is welcome news. But … it shows you how far we have to go.” Appearing before the parliamentary committee considering circuit breaker sentencing on Friday, Youth Advocacy Centre chief executive Katherine Hayes urged the government to stop using the “misleading” figure.



“The 193 per cent increase in the victims of crime refers, first of all, to the total number, not just of youth crime,” Hayes said. “So that increase in the victim numbers is almost all due to domestic and family violence, which contributes to youth crime … the use of 193 per cent hides the significance of DV in society.” In Gladstone on Thursday, Opposition Leader Steven Miles accused the government of “cherry-picking” data to convince Queenslanders things were getting better, reiterating his pledge for an independent crime data agency. World.title: Pasta-making nonnas in windows are a hit in Rome. Locals say it’s wrong
World.content:
Travel newsItaly Pasta-making nonnas in windows are a hit in Rome. Locals say it’s wrong Natalie B. Compton July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The woman in the window ignored the city foot traffic as she went about her work, her hair pulled back beneath a white hat. Her eyes tracked the strands of dough she rolled beneath her palms. Outside, a group of tourists paused to watch her toil, then one read the restaurant sign near the door aloud. “Pasta e Vino,” the woman said. And then in English: “Perfect!” Tourists wait for their order as a “sfoglina”, or traditional pasta maker, prepares fresh pasta in a window display. Getty Images Technically, the restaurant’s full name was Come ‘na Vorta − Pasta e Vino (Roman dialect for “like it used to be” or “like in the old days,” plus Italian for “pasta and wine”), but the group didn’t need to waste time on formalities. They had decided on a place to eat. Had the tourists kept walking through the sherbet-painted alleyways of Trastevere – a popular neighbourhood in Rome across the Tiber River – they would have run into even more restaurants with prominently featured pasta-makers. It’s a shtick that’s spreading across the city’s historic centre, popping up near ancient ruins and charming piazzas – and reminiscent of the other made-for-Instagram hospitality trends, like pasta served out of giant cheese wheels and saute pans.



Only this one feeds off the international appreciation of the Italian “nonna” (or grandmother) whose generational kitchen wisdom and folksy charm won over the internet. 



On a Tuesday afternoon in April, Sophie Minchilli walked her food tour through the city’s most famous farmers market in the Campo de’ Fiori. Across the cobblestone piazza, a line formed outside a restaurant where a woman rolled golden strands of pasta at a wooden table in the front window. “It’s literally like a zoo,” said Minchilli, who was born and raised in Rome. A “sfoglina”, or traditional pasta maker, rolls out dough at her station inside a restaurant. Getty Images As tourism and a demand for all things “authentic” exploded in Italy over the last decade, Minchilli has watched the pasta window trend spread. She sees their presence as a scourge - just more chain restaurants gentrifying the neighborhoods she loves and where she leads her tours. “I’ve watched these nonna-in-the-window pasta spots multiply like the Fibonacci sequence,” Erica Firpo, a writer and podcast host in Rome, said in an email. “Almost every day, I sidestep the long queues of customers.”



One of Minchilli’s qualms is that the places employing the practice tend to stay open all day and night, which can be a sign of an operation catering to tourists, who want a sit-down pasta lunch at 3 p.m. - a decidedly un-Italian move. A truly traditional establishment, she said, must close in the afternoon to give staff a break, restock and prepare for evening service. These artisans showcase the ancient art of pasta-making to tourists and locals in the city centre. Getty Images Another issue is the fresh pasta itself. “It is probably homemade and delicious, but it’s wrong,” Minchilli said. Digestion and tradition rule the Italian diet. Visiting Americans are often baffled by Italian culinary dictums, like no pairing fish with cheese, or no drinking big milky coffees after breakfast (a disaster for the stomach, they say). Pasta, too, has its own established ways. Its shape, ingredients and production vary by region.



Roman cuisine, Minchilli said, is rooted in dry pasta. Of the capital’s four iconic pastas – carbonara, gricia, amatriciana and cacio e pepe – only the latter is typically made with a fresh noodle, the square-shaped, long tonnarelli. Marina Cacciapuoti, founder of magazine and travel planning company Italy Segreta, said there’s a misconception that fresh pasta is automatically better than dry pasta. Customers dine at outdoor tables in a Trastevere alley. Getty Images “In reality, quality depends on the flour, where it comes from, and the production process,” she said in an email. “Some of Italy’s greatest pasta dishes are meant to be made with dried pasta, not fresh.” And on the contrary, “seeing someone making fresh pasta in the window is not, in itself, a sign of quality or authenticity,” Cacciapuoti continued.



You will also find great restaurants around the capital that specialise in fresh pasta from other regions. But mostly, a restaurant advertising fresh pasta as traditional Roman cuisine comes off to guide and author Katie Parla, as a red flag. Making the pasta production visible to customers? Even redder. A plate of fresh handmade Amatriciana pasta. Getty Images “If you think about it, it’s the most genius marketing tool,” said Parla, who has lived in Rome for more than 20 years. “They are providing staged content for the people. It looks photogenic. It mimics something that people perceive as authentic.” The concept of watching food preparation for entertainment isn’t new in Italy and otherwise. We’ve long enjoyed the showmanship of dough tossing at pizzerias and onion volcanoes lit aflame by chefs behind their Benihana grills. Sitting at a sushi master’s counter comes at a premium. “It’s a better than cooking show, because this is live theatre,” said Karima Moyer-Nocchi, a food historian and author of the book, The Epic History of Macaroni and Cheese from Ancient Rome to Modern America.



But Moyer-Nocchi said the pasta window trend goes deeper than entertainment. It’s a public display of “Italianità,” “the essence of being Italian,” she said. Historically, Moyer-Nocchi said, pasta was seen as a luxury for special occasions. It’s a laborious product made with ingredients “that don’t cost much now but cost a lot then,” she said. “Having it on your table meant having the time and the money to be making pasta.” Fast forward to today, and fresh pasta is once again considered a luxury. Most spaghetti eaters are not routinely making it from scratch – not even the contemporary Italian, who is as busy with the demands of modern life as their foreign counterpart, and not even the grandmas. It fuels stereotypes and misconceptions: “You’re old, you’re a woman, you are Italian, and somehow you’ve got all of this stuff in your DNA,” Moyer-Nocchi said. “Well, just like women anywhere, there are women who don’t like to cook, who aren’t capable of cooking. My [Italian] mother-in-law is just awful.” Over time, pasta-making has shifted from a kitchen chore to a symbol of Italian heritage – as romantic and impractical as singing gondoliers in Venice. And the restaurants performing that heritage tradition for their customers: “They’re selling Italy – the Italy that people long for,” Moyer-Nocchi said. “Even Italians love that idea, and it sells a lot of products to them.”



In the shadow of the Pantheon, a line formed in the Piazza della Rotonda. People were waiting for a table at Osteria da Fortunata, a chain of restaurants that serves the “flavors of authentic Roman cuisine,” its website says. Related Article Rome A local’s guide to Rome’s best places to eat and drink Fortunata’s guests dining alfresco had a postcard view of the basilica and the bustling piazza, where teenagers canoodled on the edge of a fountain. Staff in white dress shirts and black aprons - some wearing ear pieces like secret service agents - carried out glazed terra-cotta plates of tangled pasta. At the front of the dining room behind a large picture window, a woman wearing a name tag that read “Tamo” formed fat strands of dough at a wooden table. Osteria da Fortunata and Come ‘na Vorta − Pasta e Vino are the two restaurant groups leading Rome’s pasta window trend, “and we are both from the same family,” said Marcello Bettozzi, who owns the latter with his father and three brothers.



Bettozzi meant that literally. His aunt’s side of the family is behind Osteria da Fortunata, which has five locations in Rome, three in Milan one in Bologna and an outpost in Miami. Come ’na Vorta has seven locations in Rome, two in Milan and plans to expand to Spain and England. Both companies trace their origin to a great-grandmother who they say opened a fiaschetteria, which was like a wine bar, in Rome in the 1920s. Her daughter, Iris Palombi, then carried on her traditions and transformed the small establishment into a “proper restaurant,” Bettozzi said. In the 2000s, the family opened more locations, taking inspiration from pizzerias where customers could watch pizzaiolos shape dough and had staff start rolling pasta in the dining room. Soon the practice became “like a trademark,” Bettozzi said. Around this time, Bettozzi said the family split the restaurant into two brands. Both companies say they serve authentic Roman specialties made with organic ingredients, and both prominently feature a cook in the window. Bettozzi stands behind the practice, even though he insists that “it’s marketing, of course,” but it’s not a gimmick. “I think it is really important to show what we do, because people you know sometimes [people] underestimate the value of our job - it’s just pasta, it’s just cooking, you know, it is easy,” he said. “We work seven days a week, 24 hours a day, 365 days … and this finally shows a bit more what is behind [the scenes].”



(Osteria da Fortunata did not return multiple requests for an interview.) Osteria da Fortunata’s Pantheon location has a 4.7-star rating on Google Maps based on nearly 9000 reviews. The top keywords and phrases in those reviews include: “homemade pasta,” “view of the Pantheon,” “kind waiter” and “tourist trap.” Related Destination guide

Rome Rome At 9pm on a Sunday night, I joined the queue of about a dozen. Within a couple of minutes, a host came out and said the wait for a seat with a view would be about a half hour, or I could sit inside now. I took the immediate option and followed the employee into the packed dining room past Tamo at her pasta rolling station. He sent me up the stairway in the back. On the second floor, I learned the place was much bigger than it looked from the piazza. Rooms opened up into more rooms. They were as brightly lit as a supermarket.



A server with a chiseled jawline and a headset picked me off and showed me to a seat in a far corner. The restaurant churned with customers and servers, and plates of pasta coming and going. On the wall, a TV played a video interview of grandma Iris on repeat. I ordered a glass of house white wine and the cacio e pepe with fresh tonnarelli. My server warned me that the dish was “very salty and strong.” My meal came out a couple of minutes later. The wine was sickly sweet, but the pasta was decent - highly peppery, a little funky and pleasantly chewy. I’ve had better and worse. A table of four women next to me finished every last strand and tube of pasta on their plates. One let out an audible “mmmmm.” The Washington Post

World.title: As a backpacker, Martin changed my life. We found each other again 30 years later
World.content:
InspirationEurope As a backpacker, Martin changed my life. We found each other again 30 years later Kate Armstrong July 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last thing I expect when I walk into Berlin’s Hotel Adlon Kempinski is to burst into tears. My suite overlooks Pariser Platz and the Brandenburg Gate. Built by the Prussians, this neoclassical monument – topped by Victory steering her chariot drawn by four horses – is now a powerful symbol of Germany’s reunification in 1990. I’m not weeping at the scene (which is beautiful), but for the reason I’m here. I visited Berlin as a young backpacker with my friend Caroline, four months after the fall of the Berlin Wall. The wall had not yet been dismantled, which meant we still had to go through Checkpoint Charlie – what had been the border crossing between the American sector and Soviet-controlled East Berlin – and change Deutschmarks to the near-worthless East German Ostmarks. I vaguely recall the border post’s long, rectangular building. Behind a narrow, brown counter a uniformed guard placed a small slip of paper – not an official rubber stamp – into our passports. Berlin Cathedral, on the capital’s Museum Island and Spree River at sunset. Getty Images On entering the East, and with no plans, we wandered aimlessly up Friedrichstrasse until we reached Unter den Linden, a wide boulevard lined with crumbling grand mansions. Here, we lucked upon a handsome baroque building, Humboldt University, it transpired. Students around our age were pouring out of its massive iron gates. Keen to engage, we asked if anyone spoke English. A young man, his thick hair tied back in a ponytail, introduced himself as Martin. This exchange would change my life. On learning we were Australian, Martin jumped: he invited us to his English class. (“We hadn’t heard any native English speakers until then,” he explained later.) Thrilled, if a little nervous, we agreed. The class fired questions at us, mainly about our travels; until then, their travels had been restricted to Eastern Bloc countries.



After class, Martin approached us, four others in tow: “Come, we’d like to show you our East Berlin.” This six-hour jaunt was the beginning of many journeys together, including, several months later, a backpacking trip through Portugal. Given our new friends’ lack of funds, our group travelled on a shoestring: we ate market produce, camped illegally on beaches, and caught the cheaper, slow trains. It was magical. Free from their experiences under a repressive regime, they willingly reflected on the impact of the Stasi, the East German secret police. 



Out of nowhere, 30 years since our last contact, Martin tracked me down. And one year later, here I am. Back in Berlin. Our reunion at Hotel Adlon Kempinski is easy, the conversation seamless. The “whys” are left well alone. For now, at least. First, we’ll retrace our first steps through the former East Berlin. But as we start to explore, I become confused. My mind oscillates wildly between the past and the present, like a tune that loses its groove on a scratched vinyl LP and can’t regain traction. While I’m able to square this gentle, middle-aged man with the intense, athletic youth I first knew, I can’t yet reconcile the Berlin of my former experience with the city before me. I’m as hazy as the smog that used to hang over the East, the legacy of the brown coal that the “Ossis” (East Germans) burned in their fireplaces and stoves. Checkpoint Charlie, once a famous crossing point on the border of West and East Berlin during the Cold War. Getty Images The one exception is Humboldt University, where we first met. I recognise it immediately. This handsome stone baroque building remains much as it was, though it’s cleaner now, the grey exterior having been scrubbed of layers of grime. Inside the university’s airy lobby, the lingering aroma of disinfectant transports me back to Caroline whispering under her breath, “It smells like a hospital.” Back on Unter den Linden, Mercedes-Benz and other slick European cars stream past. They’re a far cry from the “Trabis”, the tiny Trabant vehicles that I recall putt-putting by, their two-stroke engines spewing sour, noxious fumes. Just beyond the university is Museum Island, a small section of land surrounded by the River Spree. We recreate our tour of all those years ago. We pose against the backdrop of the Berlin Cathedral. We climb to the top of the Französischer Dom (French Cathedral) and peer across at the Concert House and German Church. Beyond these, the cityscape is unfamiliar to me.



We wander northwest, to the historic Jewish Quarter. My yesteryear photos depict blackened buildings, pocked with bullet marks – the legacy of World War II – and piles of furniture covering the footpaths, the discards of squatters who’d moved into buildings following reunification. Today, it’s another world; even the Neue Synagogue has had a glorious makeover. The surrounding streets feature leafy courtyards, trendy restaurants, design offices and yoga studios (though scars remain; bullet marks are prolific in places). A section of the Berlin Wall is a reminder that the city and its visitors are never far from history. Getty Images As for Prenzlauer Berg, an inner-city neighbourhood, where Martin himself had “claimed” an apartment all those years ago? Gone are the grey hues, the crumbling walls, the boarded-up windows. Related Article Germany Seven highlights you need to see at Berlin’s notorious wall The decay has been eradicated. Instead, digital nomads sit in the shade outside cafes, design boutiques sit alongside bookshops and stylish, multi-storey buildings have replaced those mansions that were too dilapidated to be repaired. It’s vibrant, colourful and welcoming. Our last stop, Potsdamer Platz, is seared in my mind. I recall the Berlin Wall behind a vast void, not the buzzy commercial centre before me. A subtle line of stone blocks delineates where the wall once ran. I’m disoriented, but amazed by the transformation.



On my final evening, I present Martin with a collection of photos from our time in Berlin and our former travels together. We reminisce about the group, long since splintered. Martin is no longer in touch with Stefan, his “radical” best friend. After reunification, Stefan left Germany and cut off all former ties; it turns out his parents were full-time, paid officials of the Stasi, part of the regime he so vehemently opposed. Street life in Prenzlauer Berg, once home to boarded-up windows, now one of Berlin’s best addresses. Getty Images The Berlin city skyline with views over Tiergarten park to the Brandenburg Gate, cathedral and the so-called “red city hall”. iStock I’m sad for Stefan, but hardly surprised. So much has been written about the former Eastern bloc, including Stasiland, Australian author Anna Funder’s captivating and award-winning book. Published in 2003, it reveals much about individuals’ lives in the former German Democratic Republic. Stefan’s story is typical of so many who bear past traumas. So now is the time to hear why Martin had been silent for so long. What reason, what secret, does he have for his estrangement? I hold my breath. It’s remarkably straightforward. So mundane that I immediately write myself “out” of a Stasiland sequel. It has nothing to do with the Stasi. Nor enigmas. But simply, a former partner unable to embrace Martin’s life before they were a couple. And, in his words, Martin’s inability to handle this maturely. Now, happily re-partnered, he is reconnecting with his past. And that includes me.



So, here we are, sipping on champagne in the stunning Hotel Adlon Kempinski. It’s an appropriate place to reunite. Built in 1907, the hotel was the height of opulence during the “Golden Years” between the world wars. It partly burned down during World War II and was later demolished. After reunification, it was rebuilt in a way to reflect the hotel’s traditional design, heritage and soul. Related Article Opinion

My happy place This city became my favourite place in the world, once they got rid of the guns Ute Junker Travel writer New but old. Old but new. Just like our friendship. And the revitalised, ever-changing, German capital. Kate Armstrong was a guest of Hotel Adlon Kempinski.
